outline: Pacemaker dysfunction, including failure to sense and failure to capture
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
mechanism: Failure to capture occurs when a pacemaker delivers an electrical pacing impulse but the myocardium does not depolarize in response. On the surface ECG, a pacing spike is present without a subsequent evoked P wave or QRS complex. This differs from output failure, in which the expected pacing spike is absent; undersensing, in which intrinsic depolarizations are not detected and pacing occurs inappropriately; and oversensing, in which non-target electrical signals inappropriately inhibit pacing.
vignette: A 76-year-old man with complete atrioventricular block and a permanent dual-chamber pacemaker presents with intermittent lightheadedness. Blood pressure is 108/64 mm Hg. A 12-lead ECG shows regularly timed ventricular pacing spikes. Several of the pacing spikes are immediately followed by broad QRS complexes, but other pacing spikes are not followed by any ventricular depolarization, producing pauses. Device interrogation confirms that ventricular pacing impulses are being delivered and that ventricular sensing is intact.
lead: Which of the following pacemaker abnormalities best explains these findings?
distractor_notes: Output failure is failure of the pacemaker to generate an impulse and is characterized by absence of the expected pacing spike. This patient has clearly visible pacing spikes, including spikes that fail to evoke ventricular depolarization.

Undersensing occurs when the device fails to detect intrinsic cardiac activity, causing pacing spikes to appear despite spontaneous P waves or QRS complexes. Here ventricular sensing is intact; the abnormality is lack of a QRS response after a delivered pacing impulse.

Oversensing occurs when the pacemaker detects inappropriate electrical signals and inhibits pacing when a stimulus is needed. That produces fewer or absent pacing spikes during inappropriate inhibition, rather than visible spikes that fail to depolarize the ventricle.

Pacemaker-mediated tachycardia is a reentrant tachyarrhythmia involving a dual-chamber pacemaker and produces inappropriate rapid paced ventricular activity. This patient instead has pauses because some delivered ventricular impulses do not evoke a QRS complex.
key_expl: This is ventricular failure to capture. The pacemaker is generating ventricular pacing impulses, visible as pacing spikes, but some spikes are not followed by ventricular depolarization. NCBI defines failure to capture as delivery of a pacing impulse without an evoked potential; on surface ECG, a pacing spike is not followed by a P wave or QRS complex. The preserved output and intact sensing in this vignette specifically distinguish capture failure from output and sensing abnormalities.
objective: Recognize pacemaker failure to capture on ECG as a visible pacing spike that is not followed by the expected myocardial depolarization.
clues: some pacing spikes are not followed by QRS complexes
